unresolved_context: The target block contains bibliographic notes, copyright notices, and cataloging-in-publication data rather than prose arguments.

claims.claim: The immediate reaction to the launch of the man-made satellite was not triumphal pride, but relief regarding the first step toward escaping human imprisonment to the earth.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The immediate reaction, expressed on the spur of the moment, was relief about the first “step toward escape from men’s imprisonment to the earth.”

claims.claim: The question of whether to use new scientific and technical knowledge to alter human existence and escape the human condition cannot be decided by scientific means and is fundamentally a political question.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The question is only whether we wish to use our new scientific and technical knowledge in this direction, and this question cannot be decided by scientific means; it is a political question of the first order and therefore can hardly be left to the decision of professional scientists or professional politicians.

definitions.definition: The very quintessence of the human condition and a unique habitat providing human beings with a place to move and breathe without effort and without artifice.

distinctions.distinction: The human artifice separates human existence from all mere animal environment, whereas life itself remains outside this artificial world and connects man to all other living organisms.
distinctions.item_a: The human artifice of the world

must_not_be_lost: The characterization of modern scientific endeavors as an escape from the human condition and earthly imprisonment.
The assertion that decisions regarding the direction of scientific and technical knowledge are political questions of the first order.
extraction.segment_function: The prologue introduces the broader human and philosophical implications of modern scientific and technological advancements, specifically the launch of the man-made satellite and aspirations to escape earthly imprisonment, framing these developments as a political question concerning the rebellion against the given human condition.
unresolved_context: Details on how political institutions or citizens should address the political questions raised by modern scientific power.
The full scope of the historical transition from secularization to the repudiation of the earth.

claims.claim: The term vita activa designates three fundamental human activities: labor, work, and action, each corresponding to a basic condition under which life on earth is given.
qualifications: limited to labor, work, and action
claims.supporting_excerpt: With the term vita activa , I propose to designate three fundamental human activities: labor, work, and action. They are fundamental because each corresponds to one of the basic conditions under which life on earth has been given to man.

claims.claim: Plurality is the specific condition of all political life and is the condition of human action because humans are fundamentally alike yet individually unique.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Action, the only activity that goes on directly between men without the intermediary of things or matter, corresponds to the human condition of plurality, to the fact that men, not Man, live on the earth and inhabit the world. While all aspects of the human condition are somehow related to politics, this plurality is specifically the condition—not only the conditio sine qua non , but the conditio per quam —of all political life.

definitions.definition: The activity that corresponds to the biological process of the human body, whose conditions, growth, metabolism, and decay are bound to vital necessities.
The activity that corresponds to the unnaturalness of human existence, providing an artificial world of things meant to outlast and transcend mortal life.
The only activity that goes on directly between men without the intermediary of things or matter, corresponding to the condition of plurality.

distinctions.distinction: Labor corresponds to the biological life process of the human body and individual survival, whereas work provides an artificial world of things that transcends and outlasts mortal life.

must_not_be_lost: Vita activa comprises labor, work, and action.
Men are conditioned beings whose existence is shaped by natural and self-made conditions.
extraction.segment_function: definition

claims.claim: Aristotle distinguished three ways of life available in freedom: the life of enjoying bodily pleasures, the life devoted to the matters of the polis, and the life of the philosopher devoted to the contemplation of eternal things.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The remaining three ways of life have in common that they were concerned with the “beautiful,” that is, with things neither necessary nor merely useful: the life of enjoying bodily pleasures in which the beautiful, as it is given, is consumed; the life devoted to the matters of the polis , in which excellence produces beautiful deeds; and the life of the philosopher devoted to inquiry into, and contemplation of, things eternal, whose everlasting beauty can neither be brought about through the producing interference of man nor be changed through his consumption of them.

claims.claim: The historical shift from the ancient bios politikos to the medieval vita activa resulted in action being reckoned among earthly necessities, leaving contemplation as the sole truly free way of life.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It was, rather, the other way round: action was now also reckoned among the necessities of earthly life, so that contemplation (the bios theōrētikos , translated into the vita contemplativa ) was left as the only truly free way of life.

definitions.definition: In the Aristotelian sense, a way of life explicitly denoting the realm of human affairs and stressing the action needed to establish and sustain it.
A term that, following the disappearance of the ancient city-state, lost its specifically political meaning and came to denote all kinds of active engagement in the things of this world.

distinctions.distinction: Implied through the text's association of eternal things with contemplation whose everlasting beauty is independent of human production or consumption.

must_not_be_lost: The subordination of activity to contemplation is rooted in Greek philosophy (Plato and Aristotle) rather than originating exclusively with Christianity.
extraction.segment_function: To trace the historical evolution of the terms vita activa and ways of life from classical Greek philosophy through late antiquity and the Middle Ages, emphasizing the subordination of all action to the contemplative ideal.

claims.claim: Action is entirely dependent upon the constant presence of others and is the exclusive prerogative of man.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Action alone is the exclusive prerogative of man; neither a beast nor a god is capable of it, 1 and only action is entirely dependent upon the constant presence of others.

claims.claim: The translation of Aristotle's zōon politikon as animal socialis reflects a loss of the original Greek understanding of politics.
claims.supporting_excerpt: More than any elaborate theory, this unconscious substitution of the social for the political betrays the extent to which the original Greek understanding of politics had been lost.

definitions.definition: An alliance between people for a specific purpose, such as organizing in order to rule others or to commit a crime.

distinctions.distinction: A sharp distinction in a citizen's life between private existence and communal existence (bios politikos) made possible by the rise of the city-state.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between natural merely social companionship and the political capacity of man.
Exclusion of the merely necessary or useful from the bios politikos.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: At the root of Greek political consciousness lies a distinct separation between activities sustaining the life process and the political realm, prohibiting activities serving only to make a living from entering the political sphere.
claims.supporting_excerpt: At the root of Greek political consciousness we find an unequaled clarity and articulateness in drawing this distinction. No activity that served only the purpose of making a living, of sustaining only the life process, was permitted to enter the political realm

claims.claim: The emergence of society from the household into the public sphere has blurred the borderline between private and political and transformed the meaning and significance of both terms.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The emergence of society—the rise of housekeeping, its activities, problems, and organizational devices—from the shadowy interior of the household into the light of the public sphere, has not only blurred the old borderline between private and political, it has also changed almost beyond recognition the meaning of the two terms and their significance for the life of the individual and the citizen.

definitions.definition: A state of being deprived of something, specifically of the highest and most human of man's capacities.
A sphere whose most relevant function is to shelter the intimate, discovered as the opposite of the social realm rather than the political.

distinctions.distinction: Ancient privacy was characterized by deprivation (being deprived of the public realm), whereas modern privacy is defined by an enrichment through individualism and serves to shelter the intimate against the social realm.

must_not_be_lost: The historical transition from the ancient Greek separation of household and polis to the modern rise of society and the intimate sphere.
extraction.segment_function: explaining the Greek distinction between household and political realms, the philosophical origins of questioning it, and analyzing the historical emergence of society and the modern sphere of intimacy
unresolved_context: Specific details regarding Rousseau's rebellion against society and its connection to the flowering of poetry, music, and the novel.

claims.claim: The public realm signifies the common world of human artifacts and affairs that both relates and separates human beings.
qualifications: distinguished from our privately owned place
not identical with the earth or with nature
claims.supporting_excerpt: Second, the term “public” signifies the world itself, in so far as it is common to all of us and distinguished from our privately owned place in it. This world, however, is not identical with the earth or with nature, as the limited space for the movement of men and the general condition of organic life. It is related, rather, to the human artifact, the fabrication of human hands, as well as to affairs which go on among those who inhabit the man-made world together.

claims.claim: Mass society becomes difficult to bear because the common world has lost its power to gather people together and to relate and separate them.
qualifications: not primarily the number of people involved
claims.supporting_excerpt: What makes mass society so difficult to bear is not the number of people involved, or at least not primarily, but the fact that the world between them has lost its power to gather them together, to relate and to separate them.

definitions.definition: The world itself in so far as it is common to all of us and distinguished from our privately owned place in it, related to human artifacts and shared human affairs.

distinctions.distinction: The world is not identical with the earth or with nature as the limited space for movement and general condition of organic life, but is instead related to human artifacts and shared affairs.
distinctions.item_a: the world (as human artifact and public realm)

must_not_be_lost: Definition of the public realm as the common world of human things that relates and separates people.
The characterization of mass society's loss of the intervening world.
Augustine's principle of charity and its relation to worldlessness and familial or unpolitical structures.
extraction.segment_function: Examines the definition of the public realm as the common world of human artifacts, discusses mass society and worldlessness, and analyzes historical responses such as Christian charity and monastic rules.

claims.claim: The distinction between labor and work proposed by the author is unusual and lacks substantial support in either the pre-modern tradition of political thought or modern labor theories.
qualifications: apart from a few scattered remarks that were never developed in authors' theories
claims.supporting_excerpt: The distinction between labor and work which I propose is unusual. The phenomenal evidence in its favor is too striking to be ignored, and yet historically it is a fact that apart from a few scattered remarks, which moreover were never developed even in the theories of their authors, there is hardly anything in either the pre-modern tradition of political thought or in the large body of modern labor theories to support it.

claims.claim: Every European language, ancient and modern, contains two etymologically unrelated words for what is commonly thought of as the same activity and retains them despite synonymous usage.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Against this scarcity of historical evidence, however, stands one very articulate and obstinate testimony, namely, the simple fact that every European language, ancient and modern, contains two etymologically unrelated words for what we have to come to think of as the same activity, and retains them in the face of their persistent synonymous usage.

definitions.definition: The ancient Greek term for craftsman, corresponding to the German Handwerker.
A later term used in the polis to describe artisans, denoting men whose chief interest is their craft and not the market place.

distinctions.distinction: Every European language contains two etymologically unrelated words for these activities, and the noun 'labor' never designates the finished product or result of laboring, whereas the product itself is invariably derived from the word for work.

must_not_be_lost: The etymological persistence of two distinct words for labor and work across European languages despite synonymous usage.
The historical roots of ancient contempt for labor and physical exertion in the polis.
extraction.segment_function: Introduction to the chapter on labor, addressing potential criticisms regarding the critique of Karl Marx, proposing a neglected etymological and phenomenal distinction between labor and work, and tracing the historical evolution of ancient contempt for labor and bodily exertion in the polis.

claims.claim: Ancient estimates of human activities rested on the conviction that body labor necessitated by biological needs is slavish.
claims.supporting_excerpt: all ancient estimates of human activities, including those which, like Hesiod, supposedly praise labor, 8 rest on the conviction that the labor of our body which is necessitated by its needs is slavish.

claims.claim: Slavery in antiquity was instituted not for cheap labor or profit, but as an attempt to exclude labor from human life conditions.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The institution of slavery in antiquity, though not in later times, was not a device for cheap labor or an instrument of exploitation for profit but rather the attempt to exclude labor from the conditions of man’s life.

definitions.definition: The human species in its capacity as a laboring animal, sharing characteristics with other animal species populate the earth.

distinctions.distinction: The use of the word animal in animal laborans is fully justified, whereas its use in animal rationale is very questionable.

must_not_be_lost: Slavery in antiquity was justified by the slavish nature of life-maintaining occupations rather than being driven by a desire for cheap labor.
The modern age elevated the animal laborans and glorified labor as the source of all values.
extraction.segment_function: Examines antiquity's view of labor, the rationale for slavery, the conceptual foundations of the animal laborans, and the modern elevation of labor.
unresolved_context: Detailed mechanics of how modern economic theorists like Adam Smith and Karl Marx formulated distinctions based on productive and unproductive labor.

claims.claim: Both Adam Smith and Karl Marx shared the modern public contempt for unproductive labor, treating it as parasitical and noting that menial servants leave nothing behind in return for their consumption.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Moreover, both Smith and Marx were in agreement with modern public opinion when they despised unproductive labor as parasitical, actually a kind of perversion of labor, as though nothing were worthy of this name which did not enrich the world. Marx certainly shared Smith’s contempt for the “menial servants” who like “idle guests . . . leave nothing behind them in return for their consumption.”

claims.claim: The productivity of labor power lies not in durable external products but in the human power to produce a surplus beyond what is required for its own reproduction.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This productivity does not lie in any of labor’s products but in the human “power,” whose strength is not exhausted when it has produced the means of its own subsistence and survival but is capable of producing a “surplus,” that is, more than is necessary for its own “reproduction.”

definitions.definition: A human power whose strength is not exhausted by producing the means of its own subsistence and is capable of producing a surplus beyond its own reproduction.

distinctions.distinction: Modern public opinion, Smith, and Marx traditionally separated them by viewing unproductive labor as parasitical and leaving nothing behind, whereas pre-modern ages identified the laboring condition of household servants (needed for consumption and subsistence) with slavery because it secured masters' freedom.

The productivity of work adds new objects to the human artifice, whereas the productivity of labor power produces objects only incidentally and is primarily concerned with the means of its own reproduction and life process.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between productive and unproductive labor contains the more fundamental distinction between work and labor.
Marx's introduction of labor power as capable of a surplus was viewed by Engels as the most original and revolutionary element of his system.
extraction.segment_function: Examine the classical and Marxist distinction between productive and unproductive labor, the reinterpretation of labor power and its surplus, and the modern tendency to collapse labor into work within the perspective of the life process.

claims.claim: The distinction between labor and work becomes merely a difference in degree if the worldly character of the produced thing is ignored.
qualifications: Conditional on whether the worldly character of the produced thing is taken into account.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It seems that the distinction between labor and work, which our theorists have so obstinately neglected and our languages so stubbornly preserved, indeed becomes merely a difference in degree if the worldly character of the produced thing—its location, function, and length of stay in the world—is not taken into account.

claims.claim: The products of work guarantee the permanence and durability necessary for a world to exist, distinguishing them from the products of labor.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Viewed as part of the world, the products of work—and not the products of labor—guarantee the permanence and durability without which a world would not be possible at all.

definitions.definition: Things needed by our bodies and produced by laboring that lack stability, are consumed incessantly, and appear and disappear in an environment of use objects.

Things that are not consumed but used, to which people become used and accustomed, and which give rise to the familiarity of the world and provide the thing-character from which consumer goods derive.

distinctions.distinction: Consumer goods are needed by our bodies, produced by laboring, lack stability, and are incessantly consumed and disappear, whereas use objects are not consumed but used, giving rise to worldly familiarity, customs, and habits.
Products of work guarantee the permanence and durability necessary for a world, whereas products of labor are consumed for the life process without stability of their own.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between labor-produced consumer goods and work-produced use objects.
The role of reification in granting permanence and tangibility to the intangible products of action, speech, and thought.
extraction.segment_function: The passage analyzes the thing-character of the world, distinguishing between labor, work, action, speech, and thought, and explaining how intangible human activities and relationships require reification into durable worldly things to achieve permanence.

claims.claim: The least durable tangible things are those required for the life process, which are consumed by use or decay rapidly and return to the natural process.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The least durable of tangible things are those needed for the life process itself. Their consumption barely survives the act of their production; in the words of Locke, all those “good things” which are “really useful to the life of man,” to the “necessity of subsisting,” are “generally of short duration, such as—if they are not consumed by use—will decay and perish by themselves.”

claims.claim: Laboring activities are endlessly repetitive and bound to the recurring cycles of the biological life process, unlike working, which concludes when an object is finished.
claims.supporting_excerpt: all human activities which arise out of the necessity to cope with them are bound to the recurring cycles of nature and have in themselves no beginning and no end, properly speaking; unlike working , whose end has come when the object is finished, ready to be added to the common world of things, laboring always moves in the same circle, which is prescribed by the biological process of the living organism and the end of its “toil and trouble” comes only with the death of this organism.

definitions.definition: Specifically human life whose time interval between birth and death is full of events that can be told as a story and establish a biography.
Mere biological life shared with other living things, retaining the cyclical movement of nature.

distinctions.distinction: Bios is specifically human life constituting worldly events that can be told as a story and established as a biography, whereas zōē is mere biological life shared with other living things that forever retains nature's cyclical movement.

Laboring always moves in the same circle prescribed by the biological process of the living organism without a proper beginning or end, whereas working comes to an end when its object is finished and added to the common world of things.

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between bios and zōē
Cyclical nature of biological life and labor versus linear nature of human life, action, and speech
extraction.segment_function: Examines the relationship between labor, the biological life process, and the cyclical nature of nature versus the linear, world-building nature of human life, action, and speech.

claims.claim: Marx defined labor physiologically as man's metabolism with nature, placing labor and consumption as two stages in the cyclical process of biological life.
claims.supporting_excerpt: When Marx defined labor as “man’s metabolism with nature,” in whose process “nature’s material [is] adapted by a change of form to the wants of man,” so that “labour has incorporated itself with its subject,” he indicated clearly that he was “speaking physiologically” and that labor and consumption are but two stages of the ever-recurring cycle of biological life.

claims.claim: Locke, Smith, and Marx held that labor was the supreme world-building capacity of man, leading them into contradictions due to equating work with labor.
claims.supporting_excerpt: But all three, though Marx with greatest force and consistency, held that labor was considered to be the supreme world-building capacity of man, and since labor actually is the most natural and least worldly of man’s activities, each of them, and again none more than Marx, found himself in the grip of certain genuine contradictions.

definitions.definition: An activity that produces items meant to be fed into the human life process almost immediately, functioning as a devouring process that seizes and destroys matter.

distinctions.distinction: Labor's product is meant for immediate consumption and involves the destruction or preparation of matter for incorporation, whereas work does not prepare matter for incorporation but changes it into material to work upon and use as a finished product.

must_not_be_lost: The distinction between labor and work regarding the destruction or preservation of matter.
The historical sequence of Locke, Smith, and Marx elevating labor and encountering contradictions through equating work with labor.
extraction.segment_function: Examine Marx's definition of labor as metabolism with nature, the cyclical and destructive nature of labor versus work, labor's fight against natural decay, and the historical elevation of labor by Locke, Smith, and Marx along with the associated contradictions stemming from the equation of work with labor.
unresolved_context: Footnotes 34 through 40 referenced in the block text are not provided.

claims.claim: The emergence of nineteenth-century evolution and development theories shared a common foundational concept of process across sciences like economics, history, biology, and geology, which was virtually unknown before the modern age.
claims.supporting_excerpt: What all these theories in the various sciences—economics, history, biology, geology—have in common is the concept of process, which was virtually unknown prior to the modern age.

claims.claim: A mass society of laborers, or socialized mankind, consists of worldless specimens of the human species who are oblivious to the world due to labor's exclusive concentration on life and its maintenance.
claims.supporting_excerpt: A mass society of laborers, such as Marx had in mind when he spoke of “socialized mankind,” consists of worldless specimens of the species mankind, whether they are household slaves, driven into their predicament by the violence of others, or free, performing their functions willingly.

definitions.definition: The human condition characterized by being driven by bodily needs, concentrating exclusively on life and its maintenance, and remaining oblivious of the world to the point of worldlessness.

distinctions.distinction: The later life philosophies lost sight of the only activity necessary to sustain the life process, which was present in earlier labor theories.

must_not_be_lost: The connection between the modern concept of process, introspection, and the biological life process as a model for labor.
Marx's prediction of the withering away of the public realm and the restriction of socialized men's freedom to hobbies.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze how nineteenth-century evolution and life philosophies centered on the concept of process, linking the biological life process to labor, and to argue that neither material abundance nor socialization can overcome the intrinsic privacy and worldlessness of the animal laborans.

claims.claim: Improvements in labor tools and mute robots have eased the effort of sustaining life and giving birth, but have not eliminated the underlying compulsion of labor or the human condition of subjection to need and necessity.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is true that the enormous improvement in our labor tools—the mute robots with which homo faber has come to the help of the animal laborans , as distinguished from the human, speaking instruments (the instrumentum vocale , as the slaves in ancient households were called) whom the man of action had to rule and oppress when he wanted to liberate the animal laborans from its bondage—has made the twofold labor of life, the effort of its sustenance and the pain of giving birth, easier and less painful than it has ever been. This, of course, has not eliminated compulsion from the laboring activity or the condition of being subject to need and necessity from human life.

claims.claim: Tools and instruments used to ease labor are themselves products of work rather than labor, belonging to the world of use objects rather than the consumption process.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Tools and instruments which can ease the effort of labor considerably are themselves not a product of labor but of work; they do not belong in the process of consumption but are part and parcel of the world of use objects.

definitions.definition: Labor tools created by homo faber to help the animal laborans, contrasted with human, speaking instruments (slaves).

distinctions.distinction: Tools of workmanship result in something more than the mere use of the instrument, whereas household instruments exist for the use of the possession itself and serve the endless process of living.
distinctions.item_b: Instruments of the household / living service

must_not_be_lost: Distinction between tools of work (products of work) and labor processes.
The inherent limits of replacing living human service (slaves/household instruments) with non-living tools or gadgets due to the endless, cyclical nature of the biological life process.
extraction.segment_function: Examine the role of tools, machines, and robots in relation to labor and work, contrasting tools of work with the endless requirements of animal laborans and distinguishing the functions of production instruments from living service.

claims.claim: The ideals of permanence, stability, and durability associated with homo faber have been sacrificed to the ideal of abundance associated with the animal laborans.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The ideals of homo faber , the fabricator of the world, which are permanence, stability, and durability, have been sacrificed to abundance, the ideal of the animal laborans.

claims.claim: A consumers' society is equivalent to a society of laborers because labor and consumption are two stages of the same biological necessity-driven process.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is frequently said that we live in a consumers’ society, and since, as we saw, labor and consumption are but two stages of the same process, imposed upon man by the necessity of life, this is only another way of saying that we live in a society of laborers.

definitions.definition: The laboring activity whose ideal is abundance and whose processes are characterized by endless repetition and the metabolism with nature.
The fabricator of the world whose ideals are permanence, stability, and durability.

distinctions.distinction: Use objects possess relative durability and allow for respect and preservation, whereas consumer goods are characterized by a swift coming and going and require rapid replacement and consumption.

must_not_be_lost: The transition from a world of durable use objects to a consumers' society where everything is rapidly consumed.
The emancipation of the laboring activity resulting in its undisputed predominance over other activities of the vita activa.
extraction.segment_function: conclusion

claims.claim: Homo faber makes and works upon things, distinguishing this activity from animal laborans which labors and mixes with things.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The work of our hands, as distinguished from the labor of our bodies— homo faber who makes and literally “works upon” 1 as distinguished from the animal laborans which labors and “mixes with”—fabricates the sheer unending variety of things whose sum total constitutes the human artifice.

claims.claim: Durability gives the things of the world relative independence and objectivity, allowing them to withstand the biological needs of their makers and stabilize human identity.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is this durability which gives the things of the world their relative independence from men who produced and use them, their “objectivity” which makes them withstand, “stand against” 2 and endure, at least for a time, the voracious needs and wants of their living makers and users.

definitions.definition: The sum total of the sheer unending variety of things made and fabricated by homo faber that provide stability and solidity to house mortal humans.

The characteristic of world things that gives them relative independence from their producers and users, allowing them to endure against biological needs and wear out gradually through usage rather than through inherent destruction.

distinctions.distinction: Homo faber makes and works upon things to fabricate the human artifice, whereas animal laborans labors and mixes with things.
Destruction is incidental and occurs gradually through wearing out in use, whereas destruction is inherent and the inevitable destiny of consumer goods.

extraction.segment_function: To define the concept of work (homo faber), distinguish it from labor, and elaborate on the durability, objectivity, and stability of the human artifice.

claims.claim: The work of fabrication is guided by a mental image or blueprint that precedes the actual work process.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The actual work of fabrication is performed under the guidance of a model in accordance with which the object is constructed. This model can be an image beheld by the eye of the mind or a blueprint in which the image has already found a tentative materialization through work.

claims.claim: The process of making is entirely governed by the categories of means and end, resulting in a durable end product.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The process of making is itself entirely determined by the categories of means and end. The fabricated thing is an end product in the twofold sense that the production process comes to an end in it (“the process disappears in the product,” as Marx said) and that it is only a means to produce this end.

definitions.definition: The process of multiplying something that already possesses a relatively stable, relatively permanent existence in the world, distinct from mere repetition.

distinctions.distinction: Multiplication multiplies something that already possesses a relatively stable, relatively permanent existence in the world, whereas repetition is urged upon and remains subject to the biological cycle and the temporary needs and wants of the human body.

extraction.segment_function: An analysis of the role of models, means and ends, and multiplication in fabrication compared to the repetition of labor, along with its historical connection to Platonic ideas.

claims.claim: Consistent utilitarianism suffers from an innate incapacity to distinguish between utility and meaningfulness, trapping itself in an unending chain of means and ends without a justifying principle.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This perplexity, inherent in all consistent utilitarianism, the philosophy of homo faber par excellence, can be diagnosed theoretically as an innate incapacity to understand the distinction between utility and meaningfulness, which we express linguistically by distinguishing between “in order to” and “for the sake of.”

claims.claim: When anthropocentric utilitarianism establishes man as the ultimate end and measure of all things, it reduces nature and valuable things to mere means, thereby robbing them of their independent dignity.
qualifications: applies when man the user is made the highest end and measure of all things
claims.supporting_excerpt: if man the user is the highest end, “the measure of all things,” then not only nature, treated by homo faber as the almost “worthless material” upon which to work, but the “valuable” things themselves have become mere means, losing thereby their own intrinsic “value.”

definitions.definition: The fabricator who thinks entirely in terms of means and ends arising directly out of work activity.

distinctions.distinction: Utility corresponds to "in order to" whereas meaningfulness corresponds to "for the sake of."

must_not_be_lost: The inherent perplexity of utilitarianism in collapsing utility into meaning and generating meaninglessness.
The limitation of homo faber in understanding meaning versus instrumentality.
The paradoxical nature of Kantian formulas as rooted in utilitarian thinking while attempting to restrict the means-end category.
extraction.segment_function: Analyzing the inherent perplexity and philosophical limits of utilitarianism as the philosophy of homo faber, specifically its inability to distinguish utility from meaningfulness, its endless chain of means and ends, and its recourse to anthropocentrism and Kantian formulation.

claims.claim: Works of art possess outstanding permanence and durability because they are not subject to the destructive use of living creatures, achieving a higher order of durability that represents the stability of the human artifice.
qualifications: their durability is almost untouched by the corroding effect of natural processes
claims.supporting_excerpt: Because of their outstanding permanence, works of art are the most intensely worldly of all tangible things; their durability is almost untouched by the corroding effect of natural processes, since they are not subject to the use of living creatures, a use which, indeed, far from actualizing their own inherent purpose—as the purpose of a chair is actualized when it is sat upon—can only destroy them.

claims.claim: The immediate source of the work of art is the human capacity for thought, which transforms mute and inarticulate feelings until they are reified into worldly things.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The immediate source of the art work is the human capacity for thought, as man’s “propensity to truck and barter” is the source of exchange objects, and as his ability to use is the source of use things.

must_not_be_lost: Works of art are unique, useless, non-exchangeable objects that are removed from daily utility.
Art permanence provides a tangible premonition of immortality achieved by mortal hands within the world.
extraction.segment_function: conclusion

claims.claim: Human plurality is the basic condition of both action and speech, possessing a twofold character of equality and distinction.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Human plurality, the basic condition of both action and speech, has the twofold character of equality and distinction.

claims.claim: Speech and action reveal unique human distinctness, serving as the modes in which human beings appear to each other qua men rather than as physical objects.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Speech and action reveal this unique distinctness. Through them, men distinguish themselves instead of being merely distinct; they are the modes in which human beings appear to each other, not indeed as physical objects, but qua men.

definitions.definition: The basic condition of both action and speech, characterized by a twofold nature of equality and distinction.
In its most general sense, to take an initiative, to begin, to set something into motion.

distinctions.distinction: Human distinctness transforms the otherness shared with everything that is and the distinctness shared with everything alive into uniqueness.

must_not_be_lost: Human plurality entails both equality and distinction.
In man, otherness and distinctness become uniqueness.
To act means to take an initiative or begin something new by virtue of birth (natality).
extraction.segment_function: defining the fundamental conditions of human action and speech, specifically human plurality (equality and distinction), uniqueness, and natality as the capacity for new beginnings.

claims.claim: The revelatory quality of speech and action emerges in sheer human togetherness where people are neither for nor against each other.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This revelatory quality of speech and action comes to the fore where people are with others and neither for nor against them—that is, in sheer human togetherness.

claims.claim: Attempts to verbally express who somebody is inevitably lead to describing what he is through shared qualities, causing his unique specificity to escape.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The moment we want to say who somebody is, our very vocabulary leads us astray into saying what he is; we get entangled in a description of qualities he necessarily shares with others like him; we begin to describe a type or a “character” in the old meaning of the word, with the result that his specific uniqueness escapes us.

extraction.segment_function: An analysis of the revelatory quality of speech and action in human togetherness, the necessity of public disclosure for action, the loss of this character in modern warfare, and the fundamental intangibility of the agent's unique identity ("who") compared to descriptive qualities ("what").

claims.claim: Greek and Latin languages contain two distinct, interrelated words for the verb to act, designating beginnings and achievements respectively.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In order to illustrate what is at stake here we may remember that Greek and Latin, unlike the modern languages, contain two altogether different and yet interrelated words with which to designate the verb “to act.” To the two Greek verbs archein (“to begin,” “to lead,” finally “to rule”) and prattein (“to pass through,” “to achieve,” “to finish”) correspond the two Latin verbs agere (“to set into motion,” “to lead”) and gerere (whose original meaning is “to bear”).

claims.claim: Because action always occurs in relation to other acting beings, the actor is simultaneously a doer and a sufferer, and the consequences of action are boundless due to endless chain reactions.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Because the actor always moves among and in relation to other acting beings, he is never merely a “doer” but always and at the same time a sufferer. To do and to suffer are like opposite sides of the same coin, and the story that an act starts is composed of its consequent deeds and sufferings. These consequences are boundless, because action, though it may proceed from nowhere, so to speak, acts into a medium where every reaction becomes a chain reaction and where every process is the cause of new processes.

extraction.segment_function: Analyzing the linguistic roots, boundlessness, unpredictability, and institutional frailty of human action.

claims.claim: The Greeks did not count legislating among political activities, treating the lawmaker like a craftsman or architect whose work had to be finished before political activity could begin.
claims.supporting_excerpt: An outstanding symptom of this prevailing influence is that the Greeks, in distinction from all later developments, did not count legislating among the political activities. In their opinion, the lawmaker was like the builder of the city wall, someone who had to do and finish his work before political activity could begin.

claims.claim: Plato and Aristotle turned to legislating and city-building, which were prepolitical to the Greeks, because they wished to turn against politics and action in favor of the greater reliability of making (poiēsis).
claims.supporting_excerpt: The Socratic school, on the contrary, turned to these activities, which to the Greeks were prepolitical, because they wished to turn against politics and against action. To them, legislating and the execution of decisions by vote are the most legitimate political activities because in them men “act like craftsmen”: the result of their action is a tangible product, and its process has a clearly recognizable end.

distinctions.distinction: Making involves producing a tangible product with a clearly recognizable end and greater reliability, whereas authentic action possesses an untangible, futile, boundless, and uncertain outcome.

must_not_be_lost: The Greek distinction between the lawmaker as a craftsman and citizens engaging in politeuesthai within the polis.
The Socratic school's reduction of action to making in order to escape the uncertainty and frailty of human affairs.
extraction.segment_function: Examine the Greek concept of action, the agonal spirit, the prepolitical status of legislation and city-building, and the Socratic school's philosophical preference for making (poiēsis) over action (praxis).

claims.claim: The indispensable material factor in the generation of power is the living together of people, and whoever isolates himself forfeits power and becomes impotent.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The only indispensable material factor in the generation of power is the living together of people. Only where men live so close together that the potentialities of action are always present can power remain with them, and the foundation of cities, which as city-states have remained paradigmatic for all Western political organization, is therefore indeed the most important material prerequisite for power. What keeps people together after the fleeting moment of action has passed (what we today call “organization”) and what, at the same time, they keep alive through remaining together is power. And whoever, for whatever reasons, isolates himself and does not partake in such being together, forfeits power and becomes impotent, no matter how great his strength and how valid his reasons.

claims.claim: Tyranny rests on isolation and contradicts the essential human condition of plurality, generating impotence rather than power.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Montesquieu realized that the outstanding characteristic of tyranny was that it rested on isolation—on the isolation of the tyrant from his subjects and the isolation of the subjects from each other through mutual fear and suspicion—and hence that tyranny was not one form of government among others but contradicted the essential human condition of plurality, the acting and speaking together, which is the condition of all forms of political organization.

definitions.definition: What keeps people together after the fleeting moment of action has passed, dependent upon the unreliable and only temporary agreement of many wills and intentions, and corresponding to the condition of plurality.
An indivisible human attribute tied to the bodily existence and production of things, which is checked by the presence of others and helpless against power.
That which one man alone can exert against his fellow men, associated with the monopoly of the means of violence; it can destroy power but never become a substitute for it.

distinctions.distinction: Power depends upon the being together and agreement of many and can be divided without decreasing, whereas strength is indivisible, tied to bodily existence, and represents an individual capacity for producing things.
Power relies on human plurality and agreement, whereas force can be exerted by a single individual or a few through violence and can destroy power without ever substituting for it.

must_not_be_lost: The definition of power as generated by human togetherness and plurality rather than individual strength or force.
Montesquieu's insight that tyranny rests on isolation, contradicts plurality, and necessarily generates impotence.
extraction.segment_function: Explication of power, its dependence on human plurality and living together, its distinction from strength and force, and its relation to tyranny.

claims.claim: The traditional escape from the frailty of human affairs into stability is characterized by the concept of rule, which assumes that political community requires some to command and others to obey.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Escape from the frailty of human affairs into the solidity of quiet and order has in fact so much to recommend it that the greater part of political philosophy since Plato could easily be interpreted as various attempts to find theoretical foundations and practical ways for an escape from politics altogether. The hallmark of all such escapes is the concept of rule, that is, the notion that men can lawfully and politically live together only when some are entitled to command and the others forced to obey.

claims.claim: Plato introduced a division between those who know and do not act and those who act and do not know, separating the initiative of beginning (archein) from the execution (prattein).
claims.supporting_excerpt: Plato was the first to introduce the division between those who know and do not act and those who act and do not know, instead of the old articulation of action into beginning and achieving, so that knowing what to do and doing it became two altogether different performances.

distinctions.distinction: Plato opened a gulf between these two modes of action, which were traditionally interconnected, separating the initiative of the beginner (who rules) from the labor of those who execute orders.

must_not_be_lost: The connection between the human condition of plurality, the public realm, and the various forms of one-man rule or monarchy as attempts to eliminate plurality.
The interpretation of the history of political philosophy since Plato as an attempt to find a substitute for action rather than a tyrannical will to power.
extraction.segment_function: To analyze how political philosophy historically attempted to escape the frailty and uncertainties of action through monocratic rule and the philosophical division between ruling (archein) and executing (prattein).

claims.claim: Action possesses an enormous capacity for endurance and an unlimited process that can grow while consequences multiply, unlike the strength of the production process which is absorbed in its end product.
claims.supporting_excerpt: While the strength of the production process is entirely absorbed in and exhausted by the end product, the strength of the action process is never exhausted in a single deed but, on the contrary, can grow while its consequences multiply; what endures in the realm of human affairs are these processes, and their endurance is as unlimited, as independent of the perishability of material and the mortality of men as the endurance of humanity itself.

claims.claim: The traditional identification of sovereignty with freedom is erroneous because sovereignty, conceived as uncompromising self-sufficiency and mastership, contradicts the human condition of plurality.
claims.supporting_excerpt: If it were true that sovereignty and freedom are the same, then indeed no man could be free, because sovereignty, the ideal of uncompromising self-sufficiency and mastership, is contradictory to the very condition of plurality.

definitions.definition: The ideal of uncompromising self-sufficiency and mastership.

distinctions.distinction: Sovereignty is an ideal of self-sufficiency and mastership that contradicts plurality, whereas freedom operates within the condition of human plurality and the realm of action.

must_not_be_lost: Action has no end and its consequences are irreversible and unpredictable.
Tradition mistakenly equates sovereignty with freedom, leading to recommendations of non-acting or withdrawal (like Stoicism).
extraction.segment_function: Discusses the endurance, unpredictability, and irreversibility of action, critiquing the traditional confusion of freedom with sovereignty and identifying plurality as the condition that precludes human sovereignty.

claims.claim: Three major events marking the threshold of the modern age are the discovery of America and exploration of the earth, the Reformation's expropriation and accumulation of wealth, and the invention of the telescope along with modern science.
qualifications: cannot be called modern events as we know them since the French Revolution
motives and intentions of their precursors are still securely rooted in tradition
claims.supporting_excerpt: Three great events stand at the threshold of the modern age and determine its character: the discovery of America and the ensuing exploration of the whole earth; the Reformation, which by expropriating ecclesiastical and monastic possessions started the twofold process of individual expropriation and the accumulation of social wealth; the invention of the telescope and the development of a new science that considers the nature of the earth from the viewpoint of the universe.

claims.claim: The technological conquest of space through speed has rendered geographical distance meaningless in human life.
qualifications: finds its limit at the unconquerable boundary of the simultaneous presence of one body at two different places
claims.supporting_excerpt: Speed has conquered space; and though this conquering process finds its limit at the unconquerable boundary of the simultaneous presence of one body at two different places, it has made distance meaningless, for no significant part of a human life—years, months, or even weeks—is any longer necessary to reach any point on the earth.

must_not_be_lost: The three historical events marking the threshold of the modern age.
The historical figures and precursors are noted as rooted in tradition rather than being revolutionists.
The shrinkage of the globe and the conquest of space by speed.
extraction.segment_function: Introducing the modern age through three foundational historical events and tracing the process of world alienation and the shrinkage of the globe.

claims.claim: Galileo's use of the telescope delivered the secrets of the universe to human cognition with the certainty of sense-perception, doing what no one had done before.
claims.supporting_excerpt: What Galileo did and what nobody had done before was to use the telescope in such a way that the secrets of the universe were delivered to human cognition “with the certainty of sense-perception”;

claims.claim: Prior to Galileo's telescopic discoveries, the philosophical and astronomical speculations of thinkers like Bruno and Copernicus lacked factual confirmation and would have been dismissed as ungrounded imagination.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Prior to the telescopic discoveries of Galileo, Giordano Bruno’s philosophy attracted little attention even among learned men, and without the factual confirmation they bestowed upon the Copernican revolution, not only the theologians but all “sensible men . . . would have pronounced it a wild appeal . . . of an uncontrolled imagination.”

extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: The modern age's development was made possible by abolishing the old dichotomy between earth and sky and unifying the universe, subjecting all earthly events to a universally valid law.
qualifications: valid beyond human sense experience, human memory, the appearance of mankind, organic life, and the earth herself
claims.supporting_excerpt: this development itself was possible only because at the beginning the old dichotomy between earth and sky was abolished and a unification of the universe effected, so that from then on nothing occurring in earthly nature was viewed as a mere earthly happening. All events were considered to be subject to a universally valid law in the fullest sense of the word

claims.claim: Modern science's natural development has been underpinned by an earth alienation that surpasses the world alienation produced by expropriation and wealth accumulation or the withdrawal from terrestrial proximity.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Compared with the earth alienation underlying the whole development of natural science in the modern age, the withdrawal from terrestrial proximity contained in the discovery of the globe as a whole and the world alienation produced in the twofold process of expropriation and wealth accumulation are of minor significance.

must_not_be_lost: Archimedean point
earth alienation
universal beings
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Modern philosophy began with Descartes' universal doubt, which replaced the ancient Greek wonder (thaumazein) as the central motor of all philosophical thought.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Modern philosophy began with Descartes’ de omnibus dubitandum est , with doubt, but with doubt not as an inherent control of the human mind to guard against deceptions of thought and illusions of sense, not as skepticism against the morals and prejudices of men and times, not even as a critical method in scientific inquiry and philosophic speculation. Cartesian doubt is much more far-reaching in scope and too fundamental in intent to be determined by such concrete contents. In modern philosophy and thought, doubt occupies much the same central position as that occupied for all the centuries before by the Greek thaumazein , the wonder at everything that is as it is.

claims.claim: Cartesian doubt emerged in response to a new reality where man-made instruments like the telescope proved that neither truth nor reality are immediately given to human senses or reason without active interference.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Cartesian doubt, in its radical and universal significance, was originally the response to a new reality, a reality no less real for its being restricted for centuries to the small and politically insignificant circle of scholars and learned men. The philosophers understood at once that Galileo’s discoveries implied no mere challenge to the testimony of the senses and that it was no longer reason, as in Aristarchus and Copernicus, that had “committed such a rape on their senses,” in which case men indeed would have needed only to choose between their faculties and to let innate reason become “the mistress of their credulity.” 31 It was not reason but a man-made instrument, the telescope, which actually changed the physical world view

definitions.definition: A radical and universal doubt that occupies the central position in modern philosophy, originating as a response to the loss of self-evidence when Being and Appearance part company.

distinctions.distinction: Thaumazein was the wonder at everything that is as it is, which served as the central axis for philosophy for centuries, whereas modern philosophy since Descartes has consisted in the articulations and ramifications of doubting.

must_not_be_lost: Cartesian doubt is characterized by its universality and its departure from the traditional assumption that truth reveals itself of its own accord.
extraction.segment_function: The author introduces the rise of Cartesian doubt in modern philosophy, explaining its divergence from ancient wonder and its origins in the historical shock of scientific discoveries mediated by instruments rather than mere sense or reason.

claims.claim: The most momentous spiritual consequence of modern scientific discoveries, closely following Cartesian doubt and the Archimedean point, was the reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Perhaps the most momentous of the spiritual consequences of the discoveries of the modern age and, at the same time, the only one that could not have been avoided, since it followed closely upon the discovery of the Archimedean point and the concomitant rise of Cartesian doubt, has been the reversal of the hierarchical order between the vita contemplativa and the vita activa.

claims.claim: Modern technology originated exclusively from a non-practical search for useless knowledge rather than a pragmatic desire to improve earthly living conditions.
claims.supporting_excerpt: It is a matter of historical record that modern technology has its origins not in the evolution of those tools man had always devised for the twofold purpose of easing his labors and erecting the human artifice, but exclusively in an altogether non-practical search for useless knowledge.

must_not_be_lost: The reversal of the hierarchical order between vita contemplativa and vita activa.
Modern technology's origin in non-practical search for useless knowledge.
extraction.segment_function: Discussing the philosophical and spiritual consequences of modern science, particularly the mathematization of physics, world alienation, and the reversal of the hierarchical order between vita contemplativa and vita activa.

claims.claim: The modern age shifted the object of knowledge from eternal things or motions to processes, making history and development central to both the historical and physical sciences.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The shift from the “why” and “what” to the “how” implies that the actual objects of knowledge can no longer be things or eternal motions but must be processes, and that the object of science therefore is no longer nature or the universe but the history, the story of the coming into being, of nature or life or the universe.

claims.claim: Modern philosophy's turn exclusively to man-made things and history stemmed from despair over human reason when confronted with non-man-made objects.
claims.supporting_excerpt: The modern discovery of history and historical consciousness owed one of its greatest impulses neither to a new enthusiasm for the greatness of man, his doings and sufferings, nor to the belief that the meaning of human existence can be found in the story of mankind, but to the despair of human reason, which seemed adequate only when confronted with man-made objects.

definitions.definition: Man as a builder and fabricator, whose inherent standards include productivity and creativity.

distinctions.distinction: It is in the nature of Being to appear and disclose itself, whereas it is in the nature of Process to remain invisible and be inferable only from certain phenomena.

must_not_be_lost: The replacement of the concept of Being by the concept of Process in modern science and philosophy.
The reversal of means and ends where the production process or development is treated as more important than the finished product.
extraction.segment_function: argument

claims.claim: Characteristics of the modern age include the typical attitudes of homo faber such as instrumentalization, the means-end category, the principle of utility, and the identification of fabrication with action.
claims.supporting_excerpt: And, indeed, among the outstanding characteristics of the modern age from its beginning to our own time we find the typical attitudes of homo faber: his instrumentalization of the world, his confidence in tools and in the productivity of the maker of artificial objects; his trust in the all-comprehensive range of the means-end category, his conviction that every issue can be solved and every human motivation reduced to the principle of utility; his sovereignty, which regards everything given as material and thinks of the whole of nature as of “an immense fabric from which we can cut out whatever we want to resew it however we like”; 68 his equation of intelligence with ingenuity, that is, his contempt for all thought which cannot be considered to be “the first step . . . for the fabrication of artificial objects, particularly of tools to make tools, and to vary their fabrication indefinitely”; 69 finally, his matter-of-course identification of fabrication with action.

claims.claim: The elevation of laboring to the highest position in the hierarchical order of the vita activa was preceded by deviations from the traditional mentality of homo faber brought on by the central position of the concept of process in modernity.
claims.supporting_excerpt: What needs explanation is not the modern esteem of homo faber but the fact that this esteem was so quickly followed by the elevation of laboring to the highest position in the hierarchical order of the vita activa. This second reversal of hierarchy within the vita activa came about more gradually and less dramatically than either the reversal of contemplation and action in general or the reversal of action and fabrication in particular. The elevation of laboring was preceded by certain deviations and variations from the traditional mentality of homo faber which were highly characteristic of the modern age and which, indeed, arose almost automatically from the very nature of the events that ushered it in. What changed the mentality of homo faber was the central position of the concept of process in modernity.

must_not_be_lost: The modern shift from the what to the how and from the thing to its fabrication process deprived homo faber of fixed and permanent standards.
Man began to consider himself part of superhuman processes of nature and history without preordained telos.
extraction.segment_function: Examine the characteristics of homo faber in the modern age, the extension of the utility principle, and the subsequent historical reversal where laboring was elevated above fabrication within the vita activa due to the rise of the concept of process.

claims.claim: The victory of the Christian faith in the ancient world likely owed much to a reversal that promised immortality to those whose world was doomed.
claims.supporting_excerpt: Historically, it is more than probable that the victory of the Christian faith in the ancient world was largely due to this reversal, which brought hope to those who knew that their world was doomed, indeed a hope beyond hope, since the new message promised an immortality they never had dared to hope for.

claims.claim: The rise of Christian individual immortality as the central creed of Western mankind resulted in life on earth becoming man's highest good.
claims.supporting_excerpt: This may be the reason for the undisputable fact that only when the immortality of individual life became the central creed of Western mankind, that is, only with the rise of Christianity, did life on earth also become the highest good of man.

must_not_be_lost: Christianity's focus on individual immortality caused political activity to sink to an activity subject to necessity.
Earthly life became the highest good of man only when individual immortality became the central creed of Western mankind.
extraction.segment_function: Historical analysis of how the Christian faith's promise of individual immortality transformed the status of politics, the body politic, and the ultimate value of earthly life.

claims.claim: Marx's early consideration of world alienation in the 1842 article on the wood theft law played a minor role in his work, which remained rooted in the modern age's extreme subjectivism.
qualifications: referring to the writings and thought of the young Marx
claims.supporting_excerpt: However, such occasional considerations play a minor role in his work, which remained firmly rooted in the modern age’s extreme subjectivism.

claims.claim: World alienation is even more present in Marx's ideal society than it was before, since men will use production to objectify and actualize their true being.
claims.supporting_excerpt: In his ideal society, where men will produce as human beings, world alienation is even more present than it was before; for then they will be able to objectify ( vergegenständlichen ) their individuality, their peculiarity, to confirm and actualize their true being
